problemText: Temperature is a measure of which quantity for the particles in a sample of matter?
choices: The average kinetic energy per particle
The total energy of all the particles added together
The average speed of the particles, no matter what they weigh
The total number of particles that are moving
hints: Two samples at the same temperature share the same per-particle value — so the quantity has to be an average, not a total.
Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, so 'speed alone' cannot be what a thermometer reads.

problemText: A copper sheet is chilled in a freezer and its measured length shrinks slightly. In kinetic-molecular terms, what is happening to its atoms?
choices: Each copper atom shrinks to a smaller size
The atoms vibrate less energetically and settle closer together, while each atom stays exactly the same size
Some copper atoms leave the sheet as it cools, so less material remains
The atoms stop vibrating completely and lock into a denser element
hints: Cooling removes kinetic energy. In a solid, that energy shows up as vibration — so vibration is what changes.
Nothing was added or removed and no atom changed size, so what changed must be the SPACING between atoms.

problemText: Which statement is a postulate of the kinetic-molecular theory of an ideal gas?
choices: Gas particles lose kinetic energy every time they collide with one another
Every particle in a gas sample moves at exactly the same speed
Gas particles attract one another strongly in the space between collisions
The volume of the gas particles themselves is negligible compared with the space between them
hints: Collisions in the ideal model are elastic, and an ideal gas is defined by having no attractions between particles — so rule those two options out.
A gas is mostly empty space; that is the postulate that lets a gas be compressed so easily.

problemText: A flask holds a mixture of methane (CH₄, molar mass 16.0 g/mol) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂, molar mass 64.0 g/mol) at a single uniform temperature of 127 °C. Which comparison of the two gases is correct?
choices: The CH₄ molecules have the higher average kinetic energy because they move faster
Both gases have the same average kinetic energy, and the CH₄ molecules move faster on average
Both gases have the same average speed, and the SO₂ molecules therefore carry more kinetic energy
The SO₂ molecules have four times the average kinetic energy because they are four times as heavy
hints: Everything sitting at one temperature shares the same average kinetic energy per particle — that is what temperature means.
Kinetic energy is one-half times mass times speed squared. If the energies match but the masses differ by a factor of 4, which gas has to be moving faster?

problemText: A 2.0 g droplet of water at 80 °C sits on the rim of a 500 g pan of water at 30 °C. Which statement is correct?
choices: The pan's molecules have the higher average kinetic energy because there are so many more of them
Both samples have the same average kinetic energy because both are liquid water
The droplet's molecules have the higher average kinetic energy, but the pan holds more total energy
The droplet holds more total energy because its particles move faster
hints: Temperature is an average per particle; total thermal energy also depends on how many particles there are.
Higher temperature always means the faster particles. More mass at a lower temperature can still add up to more total energy.

problemText: Average kinetic energy is proportional to ABSOLUTE temperature, converted with K = °C + 273. A sample of argon gas starts at -23 °C and is heated until its particles have exactly three times the average kinetic energy they started with. What is the final temperature in kelvins?
hints: Convert to the absolute scale before you multiply anything: -23 + 273 gives the starting temperature in kelvins.
The starting point is 250 K, and tripling the average kinetic energy triples the ABSOLUTE temperature.

problemText: A substance is heated at a steady rate and its temperature holds perfectly constant for several minutes while it melts. Which formula gives the heat absorbed during that constant-temperature stretch?
choices: q = mcΔT, because mass and heat are still related during melting
q = mΔH, because the phase changes while the temperature stays constant
q = cΔT, because the mass cancels out during a phase change
q = mc, because ΔT equals zero and simply drops out of the formula
hints: If the temperature does not change, then ΔT = 0 and anything multiplied by ΔT gives zero — yet real energy is being absorbed.
Phase-change energy is quoted per gram (334 J/g, 2260 J/g), so the formula must be mass times a per-gram value.

problemText: Which pair of phase changes RELEASES energy to the surroundings (exothermic, ΔH negative)?
hints: Pulling particles apart costs energy; letting them fall back together returns it.
Melting, boiling, and sublimation all separate particles, so all three absorb energy. The reverse processes release it.

problemText: Ethanol has a heat of fusion ΔHfus = 109 J/g and a heat of vaporization ΔHvap = 841 J/g. A 20.0 g sample of solid ethanol is heated at a steady rate until it has all turned to vapor. Which of the two flat stretches of its heating curve lasts longer, and why?
choices: The boiling plateau, because 841 J/g is far more energy per gram than 109 J/g
The melting plateau, because melting always comes first on a heating curve
The melting plateau, because a solid holds its particles more tightly than a liquid does
They last equally long, because the temperature is constant during both
hints: Heat arrives at a steady rate, so the plateau that needs more total joules takes more time.
Melting only loosens particles enough to slide; vaporizing must separate them completely, which is why ΔHvap is the bigger number.

problemText: How much heat is involved when 150.0 g of liquid water at 0 °C freezes completely into ice at 0 °C, and does the water absorb or release it? Use ΔHfus = 334 J/g and ΔHvap = 2260 J/g for water.
choices: 0 J, because the temperature never changes
hints: Freezing is the reverse of melting, so it uses ΔHfus — the same magnitude, opposite direction.
150.0 × 334 gives the magnitude; now decide the direction. Particles falling together give energy back to the surroundings.

problemText: How much heat is required to turn 20.0 g of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 50.0 °C? Use ΔHfus = 334 J/g, c(ice) = 2.06 J/g·°C, and c(liquid water) = 4.18 J/g·°C.
hints: The trip has two stages: melt the ice at 0 °C (a plateau), then warm the liquid from 0 °C to 50.0 °C.
Stage 1: 20.0 × 334. Stage 2: 20.0 × 4.18 × 50.0 — use the LIQUID specific heat there, not the ice value. Then add.

problemText: How much heat, in joules, is needed to take 30.0 g of ice at -20.0 °C all the way to liquid water at 20.0 °C? Use c(ice) = 2.06 J/g·°C, ΔHfus = 334 J/g, and c(liquid water) = 4.18 J/g·°C. Give your answer as a number of joules.
hints: The trip crosses 0 °C, so it is three separate stages added together: warm the ice, melt the ice, warm the liquid.

problemText: Which gas law relates the pressure and the volume of a fixed sample of gas when the temperature is held constant?
hints: Look for the law whose equation contains only P and V, with no temperature and no moles in it.
Pressure and volume fight each other, so their relationship is a product held constant, not a pair of equal fractions.

problemText: A sealed sample of gas occupies 12.0 L at a pressure of 4.0 atm. At constant temperature it is allowed to expand to 16.0 L. What is the new pressure?
hints: Constant temperature and a sealed sample means Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
P₁V₁ = (4.0)(12.0) = 48. Divide by the new volume, 16.0 L. The gas got more room, so the pressure must go DOWN.

problemText: A weather balloon holds 5.0 L of gas at 250 K. It is warmed to 350 K while the surrounding pressure stays constant. What is the new volume?
hints: A flexible balloon at constant pressure means Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
V₂ = 5.0 × (350/250). Heating at constant pressure must make the volume LARGER.

problemText: A rigid sealed steel can of gas reads 3.5 atm at 77 °C. It is carried outside and cools to -23 °C. What is the new pressure inside? Use K = °C + 273.
choices: 3.5 atm — the can is rigid, so the pressure cannot change
hints: Rigid and sealed pins the volume, so this is Gay-Lussac's law: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂.
Convert first: 77 + 273 = 350 K and -23 + 273 = 250 K. Then P₂ = 3.5 × (250/350). Cooling must LOWER the pressure, and a negative pressure is impossible.

problemText: A student compresses gas in a sealed syringe at constant temperature from 10.0 L down to 2.0 L, starting at 1.5 atm. The student writes P₁/V₁ = P₂/V₂ and reports 0.30 atm. Which response is correct?
choices: Nothing is wrong; 0.30 atm is right because the particles were squeezed into a calmer space
Pressure and volume are inverse, so P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ gives 7.5 atm
Pressure and volume are inverse, so P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ gives 3.0 atm
The student should have used Charles's law, which also gives 0.30 atm
hints: Only quantities that rise together go into equal fractions. Squeezing a gas raises its pressure, so P and V move in opposite directions.
Use P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: (1.5)(10.0) = 15, then divide by 2.0 L. If your answer moved the wrong direction, the setup was inverted.

problemText: A flexible container holds 9.0 L of gas at 177 °C. It is cooled at constant pressure until its volume is exactly 5.0 L. What is the final temperature in kelvins? Use K = °C + 273.
hints: Constant pressure means Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. Convert the starting temperature to kelvins before setting up the ratio.

problemText: Which gas law is the only one that contains n, the number of moles of gas?
choices: The combined gas law, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂
The ideal gas law, PV = nRT
hints: The other three all follow ONE sealed sample from a before state to an after state, so the amount of gas never changes and never appears.
Look for the equation with no subscripts — the one that describes a single state.

problemText: At STP (0 °C and 1 atm) one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. What volume does 3.00 mol of nitrogen gas (N₂, molar mass 28.0 g/mol) occupy at STP?
hints: Molar volume is liters PER MOLE, so multiply it by the number of moles.
3.00 × 22.4 = ? The molar mass is not needed here — volume depends on the number of particles, not their weight.

problemText: What volume does 2.00 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 1.00 atm and 300 K? Use PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K).
hints: Rearrange to isolate the unknown: V = nRT/P.

problemText: A sealed sample of gas occupies 4.0 L at 2.0 atm and 400 K. Its conditions are changed to 1.0 atm and 200 K. What is its new volume?
choices: 4.0 L — halving the pressure doubles the volume, and halving the absolute temperature halves it right back
hints: One sealed sample with two sets of conditions means the combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
V₂ = P₁V₁T₂ / (P₂T₁) = (2.0 × 4.0 × 200) / (1.0 × 400). Work out the two competing effects separately and see whether they cancel.

problemText: A student wants the moles of gas in a 250 mL flask at 380 mmHg and 27 °C, and plugs 380, 250, and 27 straight into n = PV/RT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Which set of values should have been used instead? (760 mmHg = 1.00 atm; 1000 mL = 1 L; K = °C + 273)
hints: R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) carries its units with it, so it locks pressure to atm, volume to liters, and temperature to kelvin.
Convert all three: 380 ÷ 760 for the pressure, 250 ÷ 1000 for the volume, and 27 + 273 for the temperature.

problemText: At STP (0 °C and 1 atm) one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. A sealed flask holds 5.60 L of carbon dioxide gas (CO₂) at STP. What is the mass of the CO₂ in grams? Molar masses: C = 12.0 g/mol, O = 16.0 g/mol.
hints: Go volume → moles → mass. Divide the volume by the molar volume 22.4 L/mol to get the moles first.
5.60 ÷ 22.4 = 0.250 mol, and the molar mass of CO₂ is 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g/mol. Multiply.
